mainTopic: The renter's מזוזה, who owns manure in a rented courtyard, and whether a חצר acquires for its owner without his knowledge
overview: The amud opens with the end of an answer about putting a מזוזה inside a hollow reed. A ברייתא then teaches that a renter must put up a מזוזה and may not take it when he leaves a Jewish landlord's house, and רב ששת explains that the story of the punished man goes with that rule. Next the גמרא explains the משנה's ruling that manure belongs to the landlord: it is about strangers' oxen in the landlord's courtyard. This supports רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא, who says a person's חצר acquires for him even without his knowledge. The גמרא defends his rule against several challenges: lost items in an unguarded courtyard, manure caught from the air (answered by אביי and by רבא), and doves' eggs that are still subject to שילוח הקן. Along the way, רב אשי learns that renting out a courtyard without details does not include its barn. The eggs discussion ends with a minor who took them, whose father must return them because of דרכי שלום. Finally a new משנה teaches who gains when a rented year becomes a leap year, and it begins a story from ציפורי that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Putting the מזוזה inside a hollow reed
steps.stepSummary: The closing words of an earlier answer: the מזוזה is placed inside a hollow reed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Inside a hollow reed.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the last words of an answer that began before this section, about how to put up a מזוזה. It is put inside a hollow reed, and the reed is attached to the doorpost.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line finishes the earlier discussion. It explains a practical way to put up a מזוזה when the doorpost has no ready place for it, which leads into the next teaching about the renter's duty to put up a מזוזה.

keyTerms.meaning: The scroll attached to a doorpost

phrases.english: Inside a hollow reed.
phrases.notes: This finishes an answer from just before: the מזוזה goes inside the reed, and the reed goes on the doorpost.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes an answer that began before this section.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The מזוזה can be put up inside a hollow reed.

steps.title: The renter must put up a מזוזה and may not take it when he leaves
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: the renter must put up the מזוזה. He may not take it when leaving a Jewish landlord's house, but he may take it from a נכרי's house. It adds a story about a man who took it and was punished.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If one rents out a house to another, the renter must make a מזוזה for it. When he leaves, he may not take it with him. But if he rented from a נכרי, he may take it with him. There was once a man who took it with him, and he buried his wife and two sons.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with rules about the renter and the מזוזה, and a frightening story at the end.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The renter puts up the מזוזה because the duty belongs to the person who lives in the house. He may not leave a Jewish landlord's house without one, but a נכרי landlord's house does not need one. The story is placed right after the ruling about the נכרי, so it seems to go against that ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who rents out the property (the landlord)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the הלכה that a renter leaving a Jewish-owned home must leave the מזוזה in place.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who rents out a house to his friend,
it is upon the renter to make a mezuza for it.
And when he leaves,
he may not take it in his hand and leave.
But if he rented from a gentile,
he may take it in his hand and leave.
And there was an incident with one person
who took it in his hand and left,
and he buried his wife and two sons.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how to put up a מזוזה to who must put it up and whether he may take it away.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The renter puts up the מזוזה. He may not take it when leaving a Jewish landlord's house, but he may take it from a נכרי's house.

steps.title: Does the story contradict the ruling right before it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the ברייתא could tell a story that seems to go against the ruling it just gave.
steps.simpleTranslation: A story to contradict the ruling?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is surprised. The story about the punished man comes right after the rule allowing him to take the מזוזה from a נכרי's house, so it seems to contradict that rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא usually brings a story to support a ruling, not to argue against it. Since the story follows the permission about a נכרי, it looks like it is attacking that permission.

phrases.english: An incident to contradict?!
phrases.notes: The story seems to argue with the ruling about a נכרי that comes right before it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how the story fits into the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The story at the end of the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A story is brought to support the ruling before it, but this story seems to go against the permission to take the מזוזה from a נכרי's house.

steps.title: רב ששת: The story goes with the first ruling
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that the story supports the first ruling, that one may not take the מזוזה from a Jewish landlord's house.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: The story refers to the first ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת solves the problem. The story is not about the נכרי case. It shows what happens to someone who breaks the first rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man in the story took the מזוזה from a Jewish landlord's house, which the first ruling forbids. So the story supports the ברייתא instead of contradicting it.
steps.whatToRemember: The story about the punished man goes with the first ruling: do not take the מזוזה when leaving a Jewish landlord's house. Taking it from a נכרי's house is still allowed.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
It refers to the first clause.
phrases.notes: The 'first clause' is the rule that you may not take the מזוזה with you from a Jewish landlord's house.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the story to a different part of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story goes with the ruling about a נכרי, and so it contradicts it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The story goes with the first ruling and supports it.

steps.title: The משנה: manure belongs to the landlord
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: manure belongs to the landlord, and the renter gets only the ashes from the oven and stove.
steps.simpleTranslation: The manure belongs to the landlord. The renter gets only what comes out of the oven and the stove.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה about who owns the manure in a rented property. This sets up the questions that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Manure is valuable as fertilizer. The משנה gives it to the landlord, and the renter keeps only the ashes from his own oven and stove. The גמרא will next ask what exact case the משנה means.

phrases.english: The manure belongs to the landlord,
and the renter has only
what comes out of the oven
and from the stove alone.
phrases.notes: He means the ashes, which can also be used to fertilize.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Manure belongs to the landlord. The renter keeps only the ashes from the oven and stove.

steps.title: What case is the משנה talking about? The first option fails
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the משנה means. If the courtyard is rented to the renter and the oxen are his, why should the landlord get the manure?
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with? If you say a courtyard rented to the renter, with the renter's oxen, why should the manure belong to the landlord?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wants to know the exact case of the משנה. It tries one case and shows right away that the ruling cannot fit it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the renter rents the courtyard and his own oxen made the manure, it is plainly his. A ruling giving it to the landlord would make no sense there, so this cannot be the case.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with?

phrases.english: With what are we dealing?
If we say with a courtyard
that is rented out to the renter
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: and the oxen are the renter's,
why should it belong to the landlord?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what case the משנה quoted in step 5 is about.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact case where the משנה gives the manure to the landlord.

steps.title: The opposite case makes the משנה too obvious
steps.stepSummary: If the courtyard is not rented to the renter and the oxen are the landlord's, then of course the manure is the landlord's. Why would the משנה need to say it?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, a courtyard that is not rented to the renter, with the landlord's oxen. That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the opposite case and finds a new problem: the ruling would be too obvious to teach. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the courtyard and the oxen both belong to the landlord, everyone knows the manure is his. A משנה does not teach something that obvious, so neither simple case works, and the גמרא must find a case in between.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious! (a complaint that the ruling did not need to be taught)

steps.confusionAlert: פשיטא is not agreement. It is a complaint that the משנה would be teaching something nobody needed to be told.

phrases.english: Rather, with a courtyard
that is not rented out to the renter
and the oxen are the landlord's,
it is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting the first case, tries the opposite case and attacks it as too obvious.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that the משנה is about the landlord's courtyard and the landlord's oxen
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In that case the manure is clearly the landlord's, so the משנה would be teaching something that did not need to be said.

steps.title: The case is outside oxen in the landlord's courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is needed for a case where oxen from outside stood in the landlord's courtyard and left manure there.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only for a courtyard that belongs to the landlord, where oxen that came from outside stood in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 7 by giving a case where the משנה's ruling is not obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The courtyard belongs to the landlord, but the oxen belong to strangers. You might think the manure belongs to the oxen's owners or to whoever finds it. The משנה teaches that it belongs to the landlord, because it is in his courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for... (introduces the exact case a ruling is about)
The landlord, the one who rents out the property
From outside, from the world at large (not his own)

phrases.english: It is needed only for a courtyard of the landlord,
and oxen that came from outside stood in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 7 by defining a case where the משנה's ruling is not obvious.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case (אוקימתא): landlord's courtyard, strangers' oxen
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed either wrong (if the renter owns the courtyard and oxen) or too obvious (if the landlord owns both).
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה speaks of the landlord's courtyard with outside oxen, so it teaches that the courtyard owner gets the manure.

steps.title: This supports the idea that a courtyard acquires without the owner knowing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the משנה supports רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא, who holds that a person's חצר acquires items for him even without his knowledge.
steps.simpleTranslation: This supports רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא, who said: A person's courtyard acquires things for him even without his knowledge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the משנה just explained backs up a ruling of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The landlord did not know the strangers' oxen left manure in his courtyard. Still the משנה says the manure is his. That fits רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule that a חצר acquires for its owner even when he does not know.

keyTerms.meaning: A courtyard acquires items for its owner

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule that a חצר can acquire for its owner without his knowledge is an important idea in the laws of acquiring things (קנינים).

phrases.aramaic: מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא.
phrases.english: This supports Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina.
phrases.notes: The landlord never knew the manure landed there, yet the משנה gives it to him.

phrases.english: For Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:
A person's courtyard acquires for him
even without his knowledge.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the case defined in step 8 to support an outside ruling.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule that a חצר acquires without its owner's knowledge
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה, as explained in step 8, giving the landlord manure from strangers' oxen he did not know about

steps.title: A ברייתא says a courtyard does not acquire found items
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא from a ברייתא: if someone says his courtyard should acquire all lost items that come in today, his words mean nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: If someone says, 'Any lost items that come into my courtyard today, my courtyard should acquire for me,' he has said nothing. But if רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא is right that a courtyard acquires even without the owner knowing, why did this person say nothing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to go against רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the owner even wants and plans for his courtyard to acquire, and still it does not work. If a courtyard acquires even without the owner knowing, it should surely work when he says he wants it. So the ברייתא seems to disagree with רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא.

keyTerms.meaning: He has said nothing; his words have no legal effect
And if it is so (if that ruling were true)

phrases.english: They challenged: If he said,
'All lost items that will come into it today,'
phrases.notes: 'Into it' means into his courtyard.

phrases.english: 'my courtyard should acquire for me' –
he has said nothing.
And if this is correct,
what Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:

phrases.aramaic: חֲצֵרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם קוֹנָה לוֹ שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ,
phrases.english: a person's courtyard acquires for him even without his knowledge,
why has he said nothing?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא that step 9 just supported.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule that a חצר acquires without the owner's knowledge
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a courtyard acquires even when the owner does not know, then surely it should acquire when he clearly says he wants it. Yet the ברייתא says it does not.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about an unguarded courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא speaks of a courtyard that is not guarded, which does not acquire for its owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A courtyard that is not guarded.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by limiting the ברייתא to an unguarded courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule works for a guarded courtyard, where items are kept safe for the owner. The ברייתא is about an unguarded courtyard, which cannot acquire at all. So the two do not argue.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here?
A guarded courtyard, where items stay safe

steps.whatToRemember: A person's חצר can acquire for him even without his knowledge, but only if it is a guarded courtyard (חצר המשתמרת).
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא does not reject the idea that a חצר acquires. It only teaches that an unguarded courtyard cannot acquire, even if the owner says he wants it to.

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
With a courtyard that is not guarded.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the קשיא of step 10 by narrowing the ברייתא's case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case (אוקימתא): limiting the ברייתא to an unguarded courtyard
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say a courtyard never acquires found items, against רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about an unguarded courtyard, so רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule still stands for a guarded one.

steps.title: Does the unguarded-courtyard answer fit the end of the ברייתא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 11. The end of the ברייתא says that if word of the lost item spread through town, the owner's words do work. But if the courtyard is unguarded, why would news in the town change anything?
steps.simpleTranslation: If that is so, look at the end of the ברייתא: 'If word of the lost item spread through the town, his words stand.' But if we are talking about an unguarded courtyard, what difference does it make that word spread through the town?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is testing the answer it just gave by reading the next part of the same ברייתא. It looks like that answer does not fit the ending.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 11 the גמרא said the ברייתא is about an unguarded courtyard, which cannot acquire. But the סיפא says that in some cases the courtyard does acquire, once the town hears about the item. If the courtyard is unguarded, town gossip should not make it able to acquire, so the answer seems shaky.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: if your answer is right
The latter clause, the end part of a source
A courtyard that is not guarded or secured
What of it? What difference does it make?

phrases.english: If so, say the latter clause:
If word of the lost item spread through the town,
his words stand.
And if it is speaking of a courtyard that is not guarded,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי יָצָא לוֹ שֵׁם מְצִיאָה בָּעִיר,
phrases.english: when word of the lost item spread through the town,
what of it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 11 by checking it against the end of the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא speaks of an unguarded courtyard.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא says the courtyard does acquire once the town knows. An unguarded courtyard should not be helped by town news, so the answer seems not to fit.

steps.title: Town news makes people stay away, so the courtyard counts as guarded
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that once the town knows about the lost item, people keep away from it. That makes the courtyard work like a guarded courtyard, so it can acquire.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since word of the lost item spread through the town, people stay away from it, and so the courtyard becomes like a guarded courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge of Step 12. It explains how town news really can change an unguarded courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A courtyard acquires when the item is safe there. Once everyone knows the item is there and that the owner wants it, people won't take it. So in practice the item is safe, and the courtyard acts like a guarded one.

keyTerms.meaning: A guarded (secured) courtyard, which can acquire for its owner

steps.whatToRemember: An unguarded courtyard does not acquire, but if people know about the item and stay away, it acts like a guarded courtyard. So the ברייתא no longer contradicts רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא.

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דְּיָצָא לוֹ שֵׁם מְצִיאָה בָּעִיר –
phrases.english: Since word of the lost item spread through the town,
people keep away from it,
and it becomes like a guarded courtyard.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּיָצָא לוֹ שֵׁם מְצִיאָה בָּעִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains how the case changes: public knowledge turns the courtyard into a guarded one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An unguarded courtyard can never acquire, so town news shouldn't matter.
steps.terutzMaskana: Town news makes people stay away, so the courtyard works like a guarded courtyard and acquires.

steps.title: Challenge from manure caught in the air of the courtyard
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא says manure caught from the air belongs to the renter, while manure in the barn or courtyard belongs to the landlord. If a courtyard acquires without the owner knowing, the manure should belong to the landlord as soon as it is in his courtyard's air.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a challenge: 'Ashes that come out of the oven and stove, and what is caught from the air, belong to him (the renter). What is in the barn and in the courtyard belongs to the landlord.' Now if רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא is right that a person's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge, why does what is caught from the air belong to the renter? It is the air of the landlord's courtyard!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to challenge רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא again. This is a fresh attack, not connected to the lost-item ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The landlord's courtyard should acquire anything that enters it, even its air, even if he does not know. Manure falling through the courtyard's air should become the landlord's before the renter catches it. Yet the ברייתא gives it to the renter, which seems to go against רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא.

keyTerms.meaning: The air space of his courtyard

steps.confusionAlert: 'שֶׁלּוֹ' (his) in this ברייתא means the renter's, not the landlord's. The landlord is called בַּעַל הַבַּיִת.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:

phrases.aramaic: זֶבֶל הַיּוֹצֵא מִן הַתַּנּוּר וּמִן הַכִּירַיִם
phrases.english: Refuse that comes out of the oven and the stove
phrases.notes: This means the ashes.

phrases.english: and what is caught from the air
phrases.notes: Manure the renter catches in his vessel before it lands.

phrases.english: belongs to him,
and what is in the cowshed and in the courtyard
belongs to the landlord.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם אִיתָא לְהָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא,
phrases.english: And if the statement of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina is correct,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר חֲצֵרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם קוֹנָה לוֹ שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ,
phrases.english: who said a person's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge,

phrases.aramaic: קוֹלֵט מֵאֲוִיר אַמַּאי הֲרֵי הוּא שֶׁלּוֹ?
phrases.english: why does what is caught from the air belong to him?
It is the air of his courtyard!
phrases.notes: Here 'his courtyard' means the landlord's courtyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first challenge was answered, the גמרא opens a new challenge from a different ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule that a courtyard acquires for its owner without his knowledge.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Manure passing through the landlord's courtyard air should be acquired by the landlord right away, yet the ברייתא gives it to the renter.

steps.title: אביי: the vessel was held right against the cow
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the ברייתא is talking about a renter who attached his vessel right to the cow's rear. The manure goes straight into his vessel without ever being in the courtyard's air.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: It is talking about someone who attaches a vessel to the back of a cow.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge of Step 14 by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The courtyard can only acquire what actually enters its space. If the renter's vessel is pressed against the cow, the manure goes straight into his vessel and never passes through the courtyard's air. So the renter gets it, and רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: The rear (bottom end) of a cow

steps.whatToRemember: So far, the rule of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא stands: a guarded courtyard acquires for its owner even without his knowledge. According to אביי, the manure in the ברייתא goes to the renter because it never entered the courtyard's air. רבא gives a different reason in the next step.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
It is where he attaches a vessel to the rear of a cow.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי בְּמַדְבִּיק כְּלִי בְּשׁוּלֵי פָרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case of the ברייתא (אוקימתא).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The manure was in the landlord's courtyard air, so the landlord should own it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The vessel was attached to the cow, so the manure never entered the courtyard's air and the renter owns it.

steps.title: רבא: Air That Won't Be a Resting Place Doesn't Count
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers the challenge from Step 14 differently. Something passing through the air that will never land there is not treated as if it rested there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: something in the air that is not going to end up resting there is not considered as if it were resting there.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second answer to the question about the manure. The courtyard never acquires manure that is only flying through its air on the way into the renter's vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי needed a special case where the vessel touches the cow, so the manure never enters the courtyard's air. רבא says that is not needed. Even if the manure passes through the courtyard's air, it was always headed for the renter's vessel and would never land in the courtyard, so it does not count as being 'in' the courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: Airspace, the open air above the courtyard
That will not end up coming to rest there
Is considered as if it is resting there

steps.whyThisMatters: The next steps show that רבא himself was unsure about this principle in general. It is clear here only because the renter's vessel stands in the way (step 18).

phrases.english: Rava said:
Airspace in which the object will not end up coming to rest
phrases.notes: He means the manure is flying through the courtyard's air but will land in the renter's vessel, not on the courtyard floor.

phrases.english: is not considered as if it were resting there.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: אֲוִיר שֶׁאֵין סוֹפוֹ לָנוּחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different answer to the same challenge (Step 14) that אביי answered in Step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: General principle that removes the problem
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Once the manure passes through the landlord's courtyard air, the courtyard should acquire it for him.
steps.terutzMaskana: Air the object only passes through, without landing there, does not count, so the renter's vessel gets the manure.

steps.title: But רבא Himself Asked This as an Open Question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא. He states this rule as obvious, yet elsewhere he raised it as an uncertain question, in the case of a purse thrown through one doorway and out another.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this really obvious to רבא? He asked it as a question! רבא asked: if someone threw a purse in through one doorway and it went out through another doorway, what is the law? Is air where the object won't come to rest considered like resting there, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that רבא seems to contradict himself. Here he states the rule plainly, but elsewhere he asked about the same idea as a question he was unsure about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the purse case, the purse flies through a house and out the other side without ever landing. That is exactly 'air where it won't come to rest.' If רבא wasn't sure there, how can he use the idea here as a settled rule?

keyTerms.meaning: Is it really obvious to him?
He raised it as an open question

phrases.english: And is this obvious to Rava?
But he asked about it as an open question,
as Rava asked:
If one threw a purse in through this doorway
and it went out through that doorway, what is the law?
Airspace in which it will not end up resting:
is it considered as if resting there,
or is it not considered as if resting there?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי פְּשִׁיטָא לֵיהּ לְרָבָא? וְהָא מִיבְעֵי בָּעֵי לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's answer in Step 16 as clashing with his own unsolved question.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא cannot treat as obvious a principle he elsewhere left as an open question.

steps.title: The Vessel Makes the Difference
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the cases are different. In the purse case nothing stands between the purse and the house. Here the renter's vessel stands in the way.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, nothing at all is in between. Here, a vessel is in between.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבא can be unsure in the purse case but sure in the manure case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the purse, nothing separates it from the house's floor, so one might say the house's air counts. With the manure, the renter's vessel is in the way and catches it. So it is clear that the manure never counts as resting in the courtyard.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא was unsure about air an object only passes through when nothing blocks the way. Once a vessel stands in between and catches the object, it is clear that the air does not acquire.

phrases.english: There, nothing at all separates,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the purse case. Nothing stands between the purse and the floor of the house.

phrases.english: here, a vessel separates.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם לָא מַיפְסֵק וְלָא מִידֵּי, הָכָא מַיפְסֵק כְּלִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 17 by showing the two cases are different.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The purse case and the manure case are the same, so רבא should be just as unsure here.
steps.terutzMaskana: The renter's vessel standing in the way makes the manure case clear, unlike the purse case.

steps.title: Barn and Courtyard Together: Two Rulings That Clash?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the next clause of the ברייתא, which says that manure in the barn and in the courtyard belongs to the landlord. It asks how both can be true.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And manure in the barn and in the courtyard belongs to the landlord.' Two?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next part of the ברייתא from Step 14 and raises a new difficulty in its wording. The answer will come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא needs to say that manure in the barn belongs to the landlord, that suggests manure in the open courtyard does not. Yet the same line says the courtyard manure is also the landlord's. The two parts seem to point in opposite directions.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner of the property, here the landlord

steps.confusionAlert: תַּרְתֵּי does not mean the ברייתא simply repeats itself. The question is that the barn ruling seems to imply the courtyard is different, while the text puts them together.

phrases.english: And that which is in the barn and in the courtyard,
phrases.notes: This is the second half of the ברייתא about manure from Step 14.

phrases.english: these belong to the landlord.
Two?
phrases.notes: Short for: can these two rulings really stand together?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשֶׁבָּרֶפֶת וְשֶׁבֶּחָצֵר, הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת. תַּרְתֵּי?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the airspace discussion and opens a new question on the wording of the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's clause that manure in the barn and in the courtyard belongs to the landlord
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Saying the barn manure is the landlord's implies the courtyard manure is not, yet the clause gives the courtyard manure to the landlord too.

steps.title: The barn inside the courtyard belongs to the owner
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the ברייתא means one place: the barn that sits inside the courtyard. Manure there belongs to the בעל הבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: This is what the ברייתא means: manure in the barn that is inside the courtyard belongs to the בעל הבית.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question from Step 19. 'Barn' and 'courtyard' are not two places; it is one place, the barn inside the courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא seemed to contradict itself: naming the barn suggests the open courtyard is different, yet it gives the courtyard manure to the בעל הבית too. אביי reads it as one phrase: 'the barn that is in the courtyard.' So the open courtyard can belong to the renter, while the barn stays with the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means; the גמרא reinterprets the wording
The owner of the property (here, the landlord)

phrases.english: Abaye said: This is what it is saying:
And that which is in the barn that is in the courtyard,
these belong to the landlord.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא lists two separate places, barn and courtyard, which seem to contradict each other
steps.terutzMaskana: It is one place, the barn inside the courtyard, and only that belongs to the בעל הבית

steps.title: Renting a courtyard does not include its barn
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי learns from אביי's reading that a courtyard rented out without details does not include the barn inside it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: This teaches that someone who rents out his courtyard without specifying has not rented out the barn in it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי draws a practical rule from אביי's answer. If you rent out a courtyard without details, the barn is not part of the deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since manure in the barn belongs to the בעל הבית, the barn must still be his. So a plain rental of a courtyard covers only the courtyard and not the barn inside it.

keyTerms.meaning: This teaches us; introduces a rule learned from what was just said

steps.whatToRemember: A courtyard rented out without details does not include its barn, so manure in the barn stays with the בעל הבית.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical rule about what a rental includes when the contract does not spell it out.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: That is to say:
one who rents out his courtyard without specification
has not rented out the barn that is in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general rental rule from אביי's reading
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A plain rental of a courtyard does not include the barn within it

steps.title: A teaching about doves in a dovecote
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: doves of a dovecote and of an attic are subject to שילוח הקן, but taking them counts as stealing because of דרכי שלום.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: Doves of a dovecote and doves of an attic are subject to the מצוה of sending away the mother, and taking them is forbidden as stealing because of the ways of peace.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule from earlier in the sugya. This step only quotes the source; the next step explains the problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שילוח הקן applies only to birds and eggs that belong to no one. So the ברייתא assumes these doves and eggs are ownerless by Torah law. The ban on taking them is only a rabbinic rule to keep the peace.

keyTerms.meaning: Sending away the mother bird before taking the eggs
Ways of peace; a rabbinic rule to prevent quarrels

steps.confusionAlert: 'Forbidden because of robbery' does not mean the doves are truly owned. It is only a rabbinic rule to keep peace; by Torah law they are ownerless, which is why שילוח applies.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
Doves of a dovecote and doves of an attic
are subject to sending away the mother,
phrases.notes: This is the מצוה of sending away the mother bird before taking her eggs (דברים 22:6–7).

phrases.english: and they are forbidden because of robbery
due to the ways of peace.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to challenge רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule from earlier in the sugya
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule that a person's חצר acquires for him without his knowledge
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup: the ברייתא treats eggs in a dovecote as ownerless, since it applies שילוח to them

steps.title: If the courtyard acquires, the eggs should be exempt
steps.stepSummary: If a person's חצר acquires for him without his knowledge, the dovecote should acquire the eggs. Then the eggs are already his, and the פסוק 'כי יקרא' excludes owned eggs from שילוח.
steps.simpleTranslation: If רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא is right that a person's courtyard acquires for him even without his knowledge, then apply here 'If it happens before you,' which excludes what is already at hand!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the challenge. רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule would make the eggs belong to the dovecote's owner, so שילוח should not apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'כי יקרא', 'if it happens before you', meaning a nest you come across, not something already yours. If the dovecote acquired the eggs, they would be 'at hand' and exempt from שילוח. Yet the ברייתא says שילוח applies, so it seems the חצר does not acquire.

keyTerms.meaning: A person's courtyard acquires for him

phrases.english: And if it is so, this
that Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:
A person's courtyard acquires for him
without his knowledge,
read here 'If it happens before you'
phrases.notes: דברים 22:6

phrases.english: which excludes what is already at hand!
phrases.notes: Eggs that are already yours are 'at hand', not a nest you happen upon, so שילוח would not apply.

steps.triggerLanguage: ואם איתא להא דאמר רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the ברייתא from Step 22 contradicts רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule that a חצר acquires without the owner's knowledge
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the dovecote acquired the eggs they would be owned, and owned eggs are exempt from שילוח by 'כי יקרא'. Yet the ברייתא obligates שילוח.

steps.title: The obligation starts before the egg lands
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that שילוח becomes required once most of the egg has come out, but the חצר acquires it only after it falls. The ברייתא refers to that earlier moment.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: An egg becomes subject to שילוח once most of it has come out, but the courtyard does not acquire it until it falls into the courtyard. When the ברייתא says 'they are subject to שילוח', it means before the egg falls into his courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא. There is a short moment when the egg is partly out and the מצוה already applies, but the חצר has not acquired it yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two rules start at different times. שילוח applies once most of the egg has emerged, while acquisition by the חצר happens only when the egg lands. The ברייתא speaks about that window in between, so it does not contradict the rule that a חצר acquires.

keyTerms.meaning: The coming out of most of it (the egg)
As for acquiring, it does not acquire

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule stands: a חצר acquires eggs once they fall into it. שילוח applies in the earlier window, once most of the egg is out but before it lands.

phrases.english: Rava said:
An egg, from the emergence of its majority,
is when it becomes subject to sending away the mother,
but as for acquiring, it does not acquire it
until it falls into his courtyard,
and when it teaches 'they are subject to sending away,'
it means before it falls into his courtyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Steps 22–23
steps.terutzResolutionType: Timing distinction: the obligation begins before acquisition does
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The eggs are acquired by the dovecote as soon as they are there, so שילוח should never apply
steps.terutzMaskana: שילוח applies once most of the egg is out, before it lands and the חצר acquires it

steps.title: Why call it stealing if the eggs are not his yet?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא: if the ברייתא is about the moment before the egg is fully out, why does it say taking them is forbidden as stealing?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why are they forbidden because of stealing?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבא's answer from step 24. If the owner does not own the eggs yet, why does the ברייתא call taking them stealing?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said the ברייתא is talking about the moment when most of the egg is out but it has not yet fallen, so the חצר has not acquired it. But at that moment the egg is not the owner's at all. So the ברייתא's ruling that taking it is forbidden as stealing seems to make no sense.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: the opening of a challenge that builds on the last answer

phrases.english: If so,
phrases.notes: "So" means: if the ברייתא is about the moment before the egg fully came out, as רבא just said.

phrases.english: why are they forbidden because of stealing?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אַמַּאי אֲסוּרוֹת מִשּׁוּם גָּזֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer in step 24 using the ruling of the ברייתא quoted in step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's reading that the ברייתא refers to the moment before the egg falls
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the eggs are not owned yet, nothing is being taken from the owner, so there should be no prohibition of stealing at all.

steps.title: The stealing rule is about the mother birds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא's ruling of stealing is about the mother birds, not the eggs.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is about the mothers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers in one word. The ברייתא's ruling about stealing refers to the mother doves, not to the eggs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The eggs at this moment are ownerless, so שילוח הקן applies to them. The rabbinic stealing rule is about the mother birds that live in this person's dovecote. That way both parts of the ברייתא fit.

keyTerms.meaning: Their mother, meaning the mother birds

phrases.english: It is about their mother.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns which part of the case the ruling refers to
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The stealing ruling seemed to be about the eggs, which are not owned yet.
steps.terutzMaskana: The stealing ruling is about the mother birds, so it does not clash with the eggs being ownerless.

steps.title: Or: it is about the eggs, because the owner already expects them
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the stealing ruling really is about the eggs. Once most of the egg is out, the owner's mind is set on getting it, so the Rabbis treated taking it as stealing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: really it is about the eggs. Once most of the egg comes out, the owner has his mind on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another answer to step 25. The ruling is about the eggs after all, and it explains why taking them counts as stealing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By Torah law the owner has not acquired the egg yet, since it has not fallen into his חצר. But once most of it is out, he is already counting on it. So the Rabbis said that taking it is stealing because of דרכי שלום, while שילוח הקן still applies by Torah law.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: introduces a second, different answer
Really, actually: keeps the original reading
His mind is on it, meaning he expects to get it

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
Really, it is about the eggs,
and once most of it comes out, his mind is on it.
phrases.notes: "His mind" means the owner of the dovecote. He already expects to get this egg.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the challenge of step 25, different from step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the reason for a rabbinic rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the egg is not owned yet, taking it should not count as stealing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner is already counting on the egg, so the Rabbis made taking it rabbinic stealing, even though he does not own it yet.

steps.title: A new approach: the חצר cannot acquire what the owner himself cannot
steps.stepSummary: Based on רב יהודה quoting רב, no one may take eggs while the mother sits on them. So even after an egg falls into the owner's חצר, the חצר does not acquire it, because a חצר only acquires what the owner himself could acquire.
steps.simpleTranslation: And now that רב יהודה said in the name of רב: it is forbidden to take possession of the eggs as long as the mother sits on them, since the Torah says first 'send away the mother' and only then 'take the young for yourself.' Then even if the egg fell into his courtyard, it does not matter. Wherever he himself can acquire something, his courtyard acquires it for him. Wherever he himself cannot, his courtyard cannot either.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a whole new answer to the question of step 23, using a rule from רב. The eggs are not acquired even after they fall into the חצר, because the mother is still sitting on them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 asked: if a person's חצר acquires for him, the eggs should already be his, so why would שילוח הקן apply? The new answer: a חצר works like the owner's own hand. While the mother sits on the eggs, the owner himself is not allowed to take them, so his חצר cannot take them for him either. That means the eggs stay ownerless, and שילוח הקן applies even after they have fully fallen.

keyTerms.meaning: And now that he said: brings a new rule that changes how we answer
Sitting or crouching on the eggs

steps.whatToRemember: A person's חצר can only acquire for him what he himself would be able to acquire. While the mother bird sits on the eggs, he may not take them, so his חצר does not acquire them either.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a general limit on קנין חצר: it acts like the owner's hand, so it cannot do more than the owner himself could do.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַשְׁתָּא דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: And now that רב יהודה said in the name of רב:
It is forbidden to take possession of the eggs
as long as the mother is sitting on them,
as it says: 'Send away the mother,'
phrases.notes: דברים 22:7

phrases.english: and only then: 'take the young for yourself.'
even if you say it fell into his courtyard,
phrases.notes: Here the egg has fully come out and landed, which is a later moment than the one רבא talked about in step 24.

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל הֵיכָא דְּאִיהוּ מָצֵי זָכֵי לֵיהּ –
phrases.english: wherever he himself is able to acquire it,
his courtyard acquires it for him,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֹל הֵיכָא דְּאִיהוּ לָא מָצֵי זָכֵי לֵיהּ –
phrases.english: and wherever he himself is not able to acquire it,
his courtyard also does not acquire it for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַשְׁתָּא דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the question of step 23 and answers it in a new way, instead of רבא's timing answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the power of קנין חצר
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Once the egg falls into his חצר, it automatically becomes his, so שילוח הקן would not apply.
steps.terutzMaskana: While the mother sits on the eggs, the owner cannot acquire them himself, so his חצר cannot either. The eggs stay ownerless and שילוח הקן applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: It is forbidden to take possession of eggs while the mother sits on them.

steps.title: Then why only rabbinic stealing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the new approach: either he sent the mother away, and then the eggs are fully his, so taking them is real Torah stealing; or he did not, and then anyone taking them breaks the Torah מצוה of sending her away. Why does the ברייתא call it only a rabbinic stealing rule?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, how can the ברייתא say they are forbidden as stealing because of the ways of peace? If he sent the mother away, taking the eggs is real stealing. If he did not send her away, doesn't he have to send her away first!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new answer from step 28. It argues that under this approach, the ברייתא's words 'stealing because of דרכי שלום' do not fit either possible case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are only two options. If the mother was sent away, the חצר now acquires the eggs, so taking them is full Torah stealing, not just a rabbinic rule. If the mother was not sent away, whoever takes the eggs breaks the Torah מצוה of sending her away first. Either way a Torah law is broken, so why mention only a rabbinic rule? The next step answers this.

keyTerms.meaning: The ways of peace: a rabbinic rule made to prevent fights between people
He sent her away (the mother bird)
Real, full stealing, by Torah law

steps.confusionAlert: The challenge is not that taking the eggs is allowed. It is that 'stealing because of דרכי שלום' is too weak. In both cases, taking the eggs would already break a Torah law.

phrases.english: If so:
are they forbidden as stealing because of the ways of peace?
If he sent her away,
it is real stealing,
if he did not send her away,
doesn't he need to send her away!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי: אֲסוּרוֹת בְּגָזֵל מִפְּנֵי דַּרְכֵי שָׁלוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the new approach of step 28 using the wording of the ברייתא in step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The approach of step 28, that the חצר cannot acquire the eggs while the mother sits on them
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under this approach, every possible case is already covered by a Torah law, either Torah stealing or the מצוה of sending away the mother. So a rabbinic stealing rule for the sake of peace has no place.

steps.title: The ברייתא is talking about a minor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers step 29: the ברייתא is about a קטן, who is not commanded in שילוח הקן, so the only problem with his taking the eggs is a rabbinic stealing rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא is talking about a minor, who is not obligated in the מצוה of sending away the mother bird.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 29 by saying the ברייתא is about a child who took the eggs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 29 asked why there is no Torah problem: either the eggs are fully the owner's, or the taker breaks the מצוה of sending the mother away. A קטן is not commanded in שילוח הקן, so the second side of that question does not apply to him. All that is left is the rabbinic rule of stealing.

keyTerms.meaning: A minor, a child below the age of מצוות
The Torah מצוה of sending away the mother bird before taking the eggs
Literally 'son of'; here it means 'subject to' or 'obligated in'

phrases.english: It is talking about a minor, who is not obligated in sending away the mother bird.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the קשיא of step 29
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a specific person, a minor
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Whoever takes the eggs must either be stealing by Torah law or breaking the מצוה of שילוח הקן
steps.terutzMaskana: A minor is not commanded in שילוח הקן, so only the rabbinic stealing rule applies to what he does

steps.title: Can a minor be bound by the ways of peace?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the new answer: a קטן is not obligated in מצוות, so how can the rabbinic rule of דרכי שלום apply to him?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is a minor obligated in the rules of the ways of peace?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from step 30. A child is not obligated in rabbinic rules either, so how can the ברייתא say his taking is stealing because of דרכי שלום?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 30 freed the קטן from the Torah מצוה. But the ברייתא still holds that his taking is forbidden because of דרכי שלום. A child is not bound by any מצוה, Torah or rabbinic, so the answer seems to create a new problem.

keyTerms.meaning: The ways of peace: rabbinic rules made to prevent fights between people

phrases.english: Is a minor obligated in the ways of peace?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 30
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא is about a minor
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A minor is free from all מצוות, rabbinic ones included. So the ברייתא's ruling about דרכי שלום cannot apply to him.

steps.title: The father must return the eggs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the ברייתא means the קטן's father must give the eggs back to the owner because of דרכי שלום.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the ברייתא means: the father of the minor must return the eggs to the owner, because of the ways of peace.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 31. The rule of דרכי שלום falls on the child's father, who must return what his child took.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The child himself is not obligated, but his father is an adult who is bound by rabbinic rules. To keep peace between neighbors, the father has to return the eggs to the owner. This closes the whole discussion of the eggs in the dovecote.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means: the גמרא is explaining what the text really intends

steps.whatToRemember: The eggs case ends this way: a child who took the eggs broke no Torah law, but his father must return them because of דרכי שלום.

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:

phrases.aramaic: אָבִיו שֶׁל קָטָן חַיָּיב לְהַחְזִיר לוֹ
phrases.english: The father of the minor is obligated to return it to him
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the owner of the dovecote or attic where the eggs were.

phrases.english: because of the ways of peace.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר: אָבִיו שֶׁל קָטָן חַיָּיב לְהַחְזִיר לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 31 by reading the ברייתא in a new way
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting who the ruling is aimed at
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's rule of דרכי שלום is aimed at the minor himself
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule is aimed at the minor's father, who must return the eggs

steps.title: Renting a house when the year gets an extra month
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: if a house is rented 'for a year' and the year becomes a leap year, the renter gets the extra month free. If it is rented 'by months', the landlord gains, because the renter pays for the extra month.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone rents out a house to another person for a year, and the year becomes a leap year. The extra month goes to the renter's benefit. If he rented it out by months and the year becomes a leap year, the extra month goes to the landlord's benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It deals with a rental whose year turns out to have an extra month, and who gains from that month.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everything depends on the wording of the rental. If it says 'a year', the renter gets the whole year, extra month included, for the same price. If it was set month by month, each month costs money, so the renter has to pay for the added month.

keyTerms.meaning: The landlord, the one who rents out
The renter, the one who rents
The year became a leap year, so an extra month was added

steps.confusionAlert: 'Leap year' here means a Jewish leap year, when a whole month (a second אדר) is added. It does not mean one extra day.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
One who rents out a house to his fellow for a year,
and the year became a leap year,
it became a leap year for the renter.
If he rented it to him by months,
and the year became a leap year,
it became a leap year for the landlord.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַמַּשְׂכִּיר בַּיִת לַחֲבֵירוֹ לְשָׁנָה, נִתְעַבְּרָה הַשָּׁנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and topic, unconnected to the eggs discussion
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A rental 'for a year' includes the extra month at no added cost. A rental 'by months' charges for the extra month.

steps.title: The bathhouse rented in ציפורי
steps.stepSummary: The משנה begins a story from ציפורי where a bathhouse was rented using both kinds of wording: twelve gold coins a year, and one gold dinar a month.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an incident in ציפורי with a man who rented a bathhouse from another man for twelve gold coins a year, a gold dinar a month.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts telling a real story that mixes the two cases it just taught. This is setup: the story's ruling comes in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rental was described both as a yearly price and as a monthly price. That makes it unclear whether it counts as 'for a year', where the renter gains, or 'by months', where the landlord gains. The story is building toward how such a mixed case is decided.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident, a real story brought to teach the law
A gold dinar, a gold coin

phrases.english: An incident in Tzippori
with one who rented a bathhouse from his fellow
for twelve gold coins a year,
a gold dinar per month,
phrases.notes: Both a yearly and a monthly price were said, so it is unclear which wording counts.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּצִיפּוֹרִי בְּאֶחָד שֶׁשָּׂכַר מֶרְחָץ מֵחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real case that combines the two rules of step 33
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up a case where the rental was described both yearly and monthly; the ruling comes in the next part of the משנה
